1027.t: Wartime jazz concerts at Moose Hall and Orchestra Hall
1027.s: Rinker vaguely recalls jazz concerts after he left the army, sponsored by Catherine Jacobson, where he played with the Burt Kelly Stables band.
1027.ch: South Side scene and Bunk Johnson
1027.q: the Moose Hall. It was after I came out of the army and I don't remember if Bunk was there that day or not. He may have been. I know Baby Dot was there and we played together that day. Uh Bud Freeman was there. Tut's Oper. Well I can't remember who all was there. What year did that mean? Uh 1945 or…

628.t: The concert night: Bunk Johnson, Happy Goldstein as grand marshal, and the photo
628.s: Williams says Bunk played that night while Kid Howard did the advertising, that Happy Goldstein led the band on stage as grand marshal, and they look at the photos.
628.ch: George Lewis and the 1946 Jazz Foundation concert
628.q: Played that night with Funk. So Howard played that day, you know? He played the advertising. And Funk took over that night.

828.t: The 1944 National Jazz Foundation concert program
828.s: They read a concert program listing Sidney Desvignes, Teddy Wilson, Pinky's band and others, dated October 1944.

846.t: Scoop Kennedy and the National Jazz Foundation concerts
846.s: Kennedy founded the National Jazz Foundation in the early 1940s, staging Esquire-winner concerts with Bechet, Pops Foster and others, until the war ended it.
846.q: I assume that in the sense of the... the...the environment were interesting... the real stuff in the 30s, uh, I mean in the 40s, the middle 40s, early 40s came along, uh, a chap by the name of Scoop Kennedy, who is now connected with WDF, D-F-F-TV, who is an authority on cooking.

23.t: Other productions: Ellington, Hammond, Carnegie Hall, the Ivy League tour
23.s: Rose co-produced an Ellington concert and met Jelly Roll Morton through the co-producer. He brought Spanier, Bechet, Sullivan, Pops Foster and Baby Dodds to Carnegie Hall and on an Ivy League lecture tour.
23.q: And I was always prepared to discuss. I mean, I even collaborated in the production of a Duke Ellington concert one time with Rhys Dupree, who was the composer of Shorten and Bread, was the co-producer who talked me into it, and who also was the one who introduced me to Jelly Roll Morton. Mm-hmm.

377.t: First time at Carnegie Hall with Benny Goodman, and Marian Anderson
377.s: Basie recalls his 1938 Carnegie debut on 'Honeysuckle Rose' with Goodman, and hearing Marian Anderson there with Hammond.
377.ch: Carnegie Hall, nicknames and later career
377.q: Well, I can remember that -- well, I know it was a Benny Goodman concert, and it was like the first jazz concert that I heard in Carnegie and was the one I had the pleasure of being a part of it. I did a thing with Benny then on "Honeysuckle Rose."

379.s: He confirms the Afro Drums Suite concert was the first one he was asked to do.
379.q: In September. That was -- when he asked me, that's what (unintelligible).

91.t: Goffin and Feather's Jazz Music of America meeting
91.s: Carter recalls a 1942 gathering with guests of honor through a photograph.
91.q: I recall it because I have a picture that was taken at that time. But I don't really know much about it as of this moment.

383.t: Which came first: Goodman's Carnegie Hall concert or Spirituals to Swing
383.s: Wilson says Basie played Carnegie Hall in Spirituals to Swing, and he and Ted Jr. argue over dates with Hammond's concerts and an earlier 1928 concert.
383.ch: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
383.q: Jones, and it took place the same year but the Spiritual Swing Concert took place in December of 1938 whereas the Goodman Concert took place in January of 1938. So actually it did come a little later.

427.t: The first blues concert at Carnegie Hall
427.s: John Hammond's Carnegie Hall blues show with Big Bill (who took off his tight shoes), Pete Johnson, Ammons and Lewis.
427.ch: Carnegie Hall and the touring years
427.q: During World War Number Two. And, uh, we were runnin' back and forth to New York an' all over the country. Gettin' back to New York, I was uh...forgot to tell you that the first blues show that ever was at Carnegie Hall, John Hammond gave it, an' I was on the show. Had Big Bill from Chicago, a host…
